source_text:
Καὶ πῶς ἐπιβάλλεσθαι τοῦ στεφάνου
δυνάμεθα; Καλὸν ἡ νηστεία, ἀλλὰ χωρὶς προσευχῆς οὐκ ἐπιπατεῖ δαίμοσιν· «Τοῦτο
γάρ», φησίν, «τὸ γένος οὐκ ἐξέρχεται εἰ μὴ ἐν νηστείᾳ καὶ προσευχῇ.» Καὶ καλὸν μὲν
ἡ προσευχή, ἀλλὰ χωρὶς ἐλεημοσύνης εἰς οὐρανὸν ἀναβῆναι οὐ δύναται· ἀκήκοας
γὰρ τοῦ ἀγγέλου πρὸς τὸν Κορνήλιον λέγοντος· «Αἱ προσευχαί σου καὶ αἱ
ἐλεημοσύναι σου ἀνέβησαν εἰς μνημόσυνον ἔμπροσθεν τοῦ θεοῦ.» Οὐκοῦν ἡ
ἐλεημοσύνη τὴν προσευχὴν εἰς οὐρανὸν ἐβάστασεν.
thought_title: Fasting, prayer, and almsgiving need one another
orientation: The preacher is showing that each virtue is powerless without another, beginning with fasting, prayer, and almsgiving.
pass_a_gloss: And how [are we] able to lay hold of the crown? Good [is] fasting, but without prayer it does not trample on demons; "For this," he says, "kind does not go out except by fasting and prayer." And good [is] prayer, but without almsgiving [it] is not able to go up into heaven; for you have heard the angel saying to Cornelius: "Your prayers and your almsgivings went up for a memorial before God." Therefore almsgiving carried prayer up into heaven.

choices.why: The middle voice with genitive suggests reaching for or grasping the crown; 'lay hold of' keeps the physical, striving sense without over-polishing.
The verb means to tread upon; 'tramples on' preserves the forceful, victorious image of mastery over demons.
The phrase echoes Acts 10:4; 'memorial' keeps the cultic sense of a remembrance offering, and 'before God' preserves the spatial metaphor.
rejected: as a remembrance in God's presence

choices.why: The aorist of βαστάζω means to bear or carry; 'carried' keeps the image of almsgiving lifting prayer upward.

bible_refs.note: Τοῦτο γὰρ τὸ γένος οὐκ ἐξέρχεται εἰ μὴ ἐν νηστείᾳ καὶ προσευχῇ
Αἱ προσευχαί σου καὶ αἱ ἐλεημοσύναι σου ἀνέβησαν εἰς μνημόσυνον ἔμπροσθεν τοῦ θεοῦ

pass_b_english: And how can we lay hold of the crown? Fasting is good, but without prayer it does not trample on demons. For he says, “This kind does not go out except by fasting and prayer” (Mark 9:29). Prayer is good too, but without almsgiving it cannot go up to heaven. You have heard the angel saying to Cornelius, “Your prayers and your almsgiving have gone up for a memorial before God” (Acts 10:4). So almsgiving carried prayer up to heaven.

problems.source_quote: Τοῦτο γάρ, φησίν, τὸ γένος οὐκ ἐξέρχεται εἰ μὴ ἐν νηστείᾳ καὶ προσευχῇ
problems.why: Matthew 17:21 is absent from most manuscripts and appears in Mark 9:29 in the form 'This kind cannot come out by anything but prayer'—with 'fasting' in some manuscripts. The citation should likely be Mark 9:29, or note the textual issue. The brief says 'standard English Bible book names and numbering'—but Matthew 17:21 is textually dubious and typically printed as a footnote or omitted. However, the source text attributes this to 'he says' without naming a book. The English adds '(Matthew 17:21)' which may be wrong; it should be Mark 9:29 for the longer reading, or the citation is uncertain.
problems.ruling: Matthew 17:21 is textually dubious; quote matches Mark 9:29 with fasting—wrong reference misleads reader.

fixed: Changed the scripture citation from Matthew 17:21 to Mark 9:29, since the quoted saying with fasting and prayer is found in Mark 9:29 in the manuscript tradition, while Matthew 17:21 is textually dubious.

last_rejected.source_quote: «Τοῦτο γάρ», φησίν, «τὸ γένος οὐκ ἐξέρχεται εἰ μὴ ἐν νηστείᾳ καὶ προσευχῇ.»
last_rejected.why: The citation should be Matthew 17:21, not Mark 9:29.
last_rejected.ruling: Mark 9:29 also has τὸ γένος...ἐν νηστείᾳ καὶ προσευχῇ; both references valid.
